clinicalPearls: Presents as a myeloneuropathy that closely mimics the subacute combined degeneration of vitamin B12 deficiency, with dorsal column sensory loss, sensory ataxia and a spastic gait.
Recognised causes include previous upper gastrointestinal or bariatric surgery, chronic malabsorption, and prolonged parenteral or enteral nutrition lacking adequate copper.
Excess zinc — from supplements, some denture-fixative creams, or occupational exposure — is a classic and frequently overlooked precipitant, so serum zinc should always be measured alongside copper.
Zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which preferentially binds copper and sheds it into the gut lumen as cells are shed, thereby blocking copper absorption.
Haematological features — anaemia with neutropenia and sometimes ring sideroblasts or vacuolated precursors — may be misread as a myelodysplastic syndrome.
Both serum copper and caeruloplasmin are typically low, with reduced urinary copper excretion.
MRI of the cord may show increased signal in the dorsal columns of the cervical and thoracic segments, echoing the appearance of B12-related myelopathy.
Copper repletion generally reverses the cytopenias, but neurological recovery is often incomplete, so early recognition is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Copper is an indispensable cofactor for several enzymes, including cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, copper-zinc superoxide dismutase in antioxidant defence, lysyl oxidase in collagen and elastin cross-linking, dopamine beta-hydroxylase in catecholamine synthesis, and caeruloplasmin, whose ferroxidase activity is required to load iron onto transferrin. When copper becomes deficient, impaired oxidative metabolism and disturbed myelin maintenance affect the central nervous system with a striking predilection for the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, producing a myelopathy clinically indistinguishable from that of B12 deficiency, frequently with a superimposed peripheral neuropathy. Excess zinc is a common driver: it upregulates metallothionein within enterocytes, which sequesters copper and prevents its transfer to the circulation. Loss of caeruloplasmin ferroxidase activity impairs iron handling and contributes to anaemia, while direct marrow effects generate the accompanying neutropenia and dysplastic changes.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 deficiency with subacute combined degeneration
Vitamin E deficiency causing a spinocerebellar syndrome
Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urinary zinc to identify zinc excess
Full blood count with peripheral blood film
Serum vitamin B12, folate and methylmalonic acid to exclude mimics
redFlags: Progressive gait disturbance and sensory ataxia accompanied by unexplained cytopenias
New myelopathic signs in a patient with previous bariatric or upper gastrointestinal surgery
An identifiable source of chronic zinc excess such as supplements or denture-fixative cream
Worsening myelopathy despite a normal vitamin B12 level
reference.prognosis: Haematological abnormalities usually correct promptly once copper is replaced, but neurological deficits often only stabilise rather than fully resolve. Outcome is best when the diagnosis is made early and the underlying cause, particularly zinc excess, is corrected.
pitfalls: Anchoring on B12 deficiency and abandoning the work-up once B12 is found to be normal.
Failing to seek a source of zinc excess, especially denture-fixative creams.
Misinterpreting the marrow and blood-film changes as a primary myelodysplastic syndrome.
Reassuring patients that neurological deficits will completely resolve with treatment.
management: Copper repletion is the definitive treatment, given orally when tolerated or intravenously in malabsorption or severe deficiency, to arrest neurological decline
Identify and eliminate zinc excess from supplements, denture creams or occupational exposure, the classic reversible driver
Correct chronic malabsorption and ensure adequate copper content in prolonged parenteral or enteral nutrition
Monitor response with serial serum copper, caeruloplasmin and full blood count until normalised
Exclude vitamin B12 deficiency as the main mimic and treat if coexistent
Provide neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for sensory ataxia, spasticity and gait impairment
Refer jointly to neurology and metabolic medicine, counselling that haematological abnormalities usually correct but established neurological deficits may only stabilise
